title: Lambda Labs Pricing: GPU Cost Per Hour (2026 Guide)
summary: Lambda Labs pricing is charged per GPU-hour, varying by instance type. Find the specific cost for each GPU model to fit your training budget.
body_markdown:
## Frequently asked questions


### Does Lambda Labs charge when an instance is stopped?


I can't confirm a stopped-instance billing rule from what I've verified, so check Lambda's current billing page before you rely on one.


What I can say is that the line item that bites is usually the persistent storage attached to your work, which stays on the invoice whether or not a GPU is running.


That means a "paused" project can keep costing you quietly, so audit what's attached before you walk away from it.


Is there a free tier or free credit on Lambda? I have no confirmed free tier or credit program to point you to, and promotional offers change often enough that anything I told you could be stale.


Look at the current sign-up and pricing pages. Treat any credit as a way to test real workloads, including storage and startup time, rather than as a reason to pick a plan.


### Can I get a discount for a long-term commitment?


Lambda has offered reserved and committed arrangements, but I won't quote terms I can't verify. The useful question is what happens if your usage drops: a commitment lowers the hourly rate and raises the cost of being wrong.


Read the clauses on early exit and on changing GPU type before you sign, because those decide whether the discount holds up.


Has Lambda Labs changed its name or domain? I can't verify a rename or a domain change, so I won't claim one.


If you're following an old tutorial, a stale link or an outdated product name is a good reason to start from Lambda's current site and the account you actually hold, not from a bookmark.


### Which Lambda GPU is cheapest for fine-tuning a 7B model?


Rarely is the cheapest GPU per hour the cheapest for the job. A 7B fine-tune that fits comfortably in memory on a mid-range card, using parameter-efficient methods, will usually cost less than a bigger card that finishes sooner but sits idle while you debug.


Pick the smallest GPU that holds your model and batch size without out-of-memory restarts, then compare total cost per finished run, not the rate on the listing.
